newsitem.title: BELGIUM: German BSE case not to delay end of UK beef ban.
newsitem.headline: German BSE case not to delay end of UK beef ban.

text.p: A new case of mad cow disease, the first which could involve an animal born of British stock in Germany, should not make it more difficult to ease a worldwide ban on British beef, EU and industry officials said on Thursday.

"The latest case does not add any new scientific evidence," a European Union official said, noting that EU scientists were analysing a British report on the transmission of the disease, Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), from cows to calves.

On Wednesday, German officials ordered the immediate slaughter of 5,200 cattle imported from Britain and Switzerland where the greatest number of cases , have been reported. They also urged the monitoring of 14,000 offspring.

The scientists are expected to report in March on the study, first announced on August 1, 1996, which found that maternal transmission was possible but at a rate of one percent of the total national herd.
If confirmed, it would add to pressure to cull more cattle both in Britain and on the continent to protect public health.
But an official at the EU farmers' organisation COPA said it was uncertain whether the case was an example of maternal transmission as Germany says.

The official said BSE had never been confirmed in cattle under 30 months of age while Britain had culled over one million animals over that age, which had eaten contaminated feed containing meat and bone meal before it was banned.
"If the selective slaughter programme is implemented then no new extra measures are needed," the official said, adding that there was no reason to hold up a step by step easing of the ban.
German state agriculture secretary Franz-Josef Feiter said in Bonn on Wednesday that the origin of the cow was uncertain as its ear-tag appeared to have been altered.
Feiter added that the case was baffling as the presumed mother, slaughtered last year, had shown no signs of BSE.

The case was the fifth confirmed in Germany, all involving cattle of British origin, but the first since since the BSE crisis broke in March 1996 after Britain admitted that people eating infected beef could develop Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease, the human equivalent of the fatal animal brain-wasting disease.
Germany, where consumers are particularly sensitive to public health issues, has been at the forefront of countries wanting tough action over BSE.
It has refused to agree to any easing of the export ban, even passing its own legislation to block an EU decision allowing Britain to resume exports of bull semen.
Britain is due to present detailed plans to the European Commission in early February for the selective slaughter of some 100,000 cattle most at risk to BSE.
The selective slaughter programme is part of a compromise to end the mad cow crisis hammered out by EU leaders in Florence last June.
